01.note: Mar Ukva had a poor neighbor, and every day he secretly tossed four dinars for him through a slot by the hinge of his door. One day the poor man decided to find out who was doing him this kindness. That day Mar Ukva was late from the study hall and his wife came with him. When the poor man came out after them, they ran and hid in a furnace whose fire had been raked over but was still burning. Mar Ukva's legs were being singed, and his wife told him to rest his feet on hers. He became distraught, and she explained: she is at home, and the help she gives reaches the poor directly.
01.why: The Gemara has been discussing how charity should treat a poor man who refuses help, and now tells stories of how the Sages gave. It explains their flight into the furnace with a teaching: better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to shame another person in public.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Gave charity every day to a poor neighbor without letting him know who the giver was.

people.name: Mar Ukva's wife
people.about: Came with him that day; her legs were spared in the furnace, and she explained why.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
The house of study where the Sages learned Torah together.

02.note: Mar Ukva used to send four hundred dinars every year, on the eve of Yom Kippur, to a poor man in his neighborhood. One year he sent the money with his son, who came back and said the man did not need it: he had seen the household sprinkling old wine for him, which the translation explains was to scent the room. Mar Ukva said: he is that pampered? He doubled the sum and sent it to him.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting stories of how the Sages gave charity. In the very next story Rabbi Ḥanina's wife reports signs of wealth and he concludes the man is not needy; here the same kind of report leads Mar Ukva to give more.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Sent a yearly gift of charity to a poor neighbor.

people.name: Mar Ukva's son
people.about: Carried the money one year and reported that the man did not need it.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
A silver coin.

03.note: When Mar Ukva was dying, he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said: My provisions are light and the way is far, meaning, as the translation explains, that this was too little to bring him to the World to Come. He got up and gave away half of all his money.
03.why: The Gemara uses the story to raise a ruling made at Usha that no one should give away more than a fifth of his wealth, and answers that the limit protects a living person from becoming poor and does not apply at death.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A generous giver of charity, reviewing his record as he was dying.

people.name: Rabbi Ilai
people.about: The Sage who reports the Usha ruling limiting charity to a fifth of one's wealth.

terms.meaning: A town where the Sages met and enacted a set of ordinances.
The life after this one, in which a person is rewarded for his deeds.
Fine gold coins, according to the translation.

04.note: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a letter that opened, Huna, our friend, peace! and asked him to give a woman one-tenth of her father's estate. Rav Huna told Rav Sheshet, who was sitting before him, to carry back a reply, and put anyone who failed to say it under a ban: Anan, Anan! From land or from movable property? And who sits at the head in the house of a marzeiḥa? Rav Sheshet delivered it word for word, saying he would never have spoken so to a teacher except for the ban. Rav Anan took the message to Mar Ukva, admitting he did not know what a marzeiḥa was. Mar Ukva heard the whole story and said: a man who does not know what a marzeiḥa is writes to Rav Huna as Huna, our friend?
04.why: The Gemara is discussing a daughter's right to a tenth of her father's estate for her dowry, and from what it is paid. Rav Huna's barbed question raises exactly that point, which Rava settles after the story: from land, not movable property.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Wrote to Rav Huna as an equal on behalf of a woman claiming her share of an estate.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Took offense at the familiar greeting and sent a sharp reply.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sat before Rav Huna and was made to deliver his reply.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Rav Anan turned to him for advice and told him he had overstepped.

terms.meaning: The Gemara explains it means a mourner, citing Jeremiah's words about a house of mourning. The point of the question was who sits at the head among mourners.
Excommunication: a formal ban a Sage could place on someone, cutting him off from the community.
Goods and money, as opposed to land.

05.note: Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and declared: if anyone brings me a teaching from the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya and I cannot show it in the Mishna, I will fall and drown. The translation explains that he did this after Rabbi Yoḥanan was made head of the academy in his absence. An old man came and taught: if a dying man says, Give my sons a shekel a week, and they need a sela, they get a sela; if he said, Give them only a shekel, they get only a shekel; and if he said that others should inherit after them, they get only a shekel either way. Ilfa answered that this follows Rabbi Meir, who says it is a mitzva to carry out the words of the dead.
05.why: Just before, the Gemara reads the mishna as a dispute in which Rabbi Meir holds that a third party must carry out a dead father's instructions about his daughter's money. Ilfa traces the old man's teaching to that same view of Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: A Sage who staked his life on tracing any teaching back to the Mishna.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: His school's teachings were the challenge Ilfa invited.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Named with Rabbi Ḥiyya as the source of the teachings.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose view, that the words of the dead must be carried out, Ilfa cites.

terms.meaning: The core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.
Coins; according to the translation a sela is worth two shekels.
A religious duty.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

05.flag: The last two STORY segments are not part of Ilfa's story: one is Rav Ḥisda's ruling on the shekel case with the Gemara's discussion, the other quotes a mishna about children's sales that opens the next topic.

06.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥanna recalled walking behind Rav Ukva when he saw an Arab woman sitting, casting her spindle and spinning red thread opposite her face. When she saw them, she broke the spindle off the thread and threw it down, and said to him: Young man, give me the spindle. Rav Ukva said something about her. Later Sages disagreed about what he said: Ravina said he called her an example of a woman who spins in the marketplace; the Rabbis said, of a woman who speaks with every man.
06.why: The mishna lists conduct that breaks the customs of Jewish women, including spinning in the marketplace and speaking with every man, and Avimi has just explained spinning as working red thread before one's face. This encounter is offered as such a scene.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥanna
people.about: Tells the story; he was walking behind Rav Ukva.

people.name: Rav Ukva
people.about: Made a remark about the woman.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A later Sage who explained what Rav Ukva's remark was.

terms.meaning: A weighted stick that is spun to twist fibers into thread.

07.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan warned people to beware the flies of those with ra'atan, and other Sages kept their distance from the sick, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi stayed close to them and studied Torah, saying the Torah protects those who learn it. As he was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his will. He asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the angel's knife on the way; when shown his place, he jumped in. The angel grabbed his cloak, but he swore he would not come back, and God ruled he could stay since he had never had an oath released. He kept the knife until a Divine Voice ordered him to return it. Elijah announced him, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked if a rainbow had been seen in his days. He said yes; the Gemara says none had been, but he would not take credit.
07.why: The Gemara has been describing the disease ra'atan and its cure. This story sets the Sages who avoided its sufferers against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who stayed with them, and the next story names that devotion as the merit that set him apart.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Warned people about the flies of those with ra'atan.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Studied Torah beside the sick and outwitted the Angel of Death.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: Sent to take Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and tricked out of his knife.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who announced Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's arrival in paradise.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Found sitting on thirteen golden stools in paradise; he questioned the newcomer.

terms.meaning: A severe disease the Gemara describes: watering eyes, running nose, drooling, and flies resting on the sufferer.
A voice from heaven that speaks in the Talmud's stories.
The translation explains that a rainbow signals the world deserves a flood, so none appears in the lifetime of a completely righteous man.

08.note: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa was a friend of the Angel of Death. When he was dying, the angel was told to do his will. He asked for thirty days to review his learning, since happy is the one who arrives with his learning in hand, and got them. Then he asked to see his place and to hold the angel's knife. The angel asked whether he meant to do what his friend had done. Rabbi Ḥanina said: bring a Torah scroll and see if there is anything in it I have not kept. The angel asked: did you stay close to those with ra'atan and study Torah? Even so, when he died a pillar of fire separated him from everyone. Rabbi Alexandri asked it to withdraw in honor of the Sages, then of his father, with no effect; in his own honor, it withdrew.
08.why: It follows straight on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's escape and measures Rabbi Ḥanina against him: without that devotion to the sick he cannot repeat the trick, yet still receives a rare honor. Abaye and Rav Adda bar Mattana then argue over what the pillar meant.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage and friend of the Angel of Death who tried to enter paradise alive.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: Sent to take him, and wary of being tricked again.

people.name: Rabbi Alexandri
people.about: Persuaded the pillar of fire to withdraw.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Said the pillar set Rabbi Ḥanina apart from those who had not kept the Torah.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Answered Abaye with a jab that Abaye's roof had no guardrail.

terms.meaning: A severe disease; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had studied Torah beside its sufferers.
By the Gemara's tradition, a pillar of fire separates only one or two people in a generation.
The Torah requires a railing around a flat roof; the Gemara says Abaye had one, but the wind had just blown it down.

09.note: A woman who wanted to keep her property out of her husband's hands wrote it over to her daughter. She married and was divorced, and the case came before Rav Naḥman, who tore up the deed. Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva: see how Naḥman the farmer tears up people's documents! Mar Ukva asked for the details, then said: you mean a document of evasion? Shmuel said that if such a document came into his hands he would tear it up. Rava asked Rav Naḥman his reason: a person does not give away his own property to others, but surely a mother gives to her daughter? Rav Naḥman answered: even against her daughter, a woman puts herself first.
09.why: The Gemara is discussing a woman's power to sell or give away her property beyond her husband's reach. This case asks whether a deed made only to shield property from a husband is real, and the Gemara then challenges it from a baraita that seems to uphold such deeds.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who tore up the woman's deed of gift.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Objected to Rav Naḥman's ruling.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Heard Rav Anan's complaint and backed the ruling; the translation calls him the Exilarch.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Earlier Sage quoted as saying he would tear up any document of evasion.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Asked Rav Naḥman for the reason behind his ruling.

terms.meaning: A deed written only to keep property away from someone, here a husband, not meant as a real gift.

10.note: A woman inherited four hundred dinars in Bei Ḥozai. Her husband went to collect it, spent six hundred of his own on the journey, and brought back the four hundred; on the way home he needed one dinar and took it from her money. He came before Rabbi Ami, who said: what he spent, he spent, and what he ate, he ate. The Sages objected that this rule applies when a husband eats the produce of his wife's property, but here he took from the principal, and that counts as an expense. Rabbi Ami replied: then he spent and did not eat, so he takes an oath on how much he spent and recovers it.
10.why: The mishna lets a husband who spent on his wife's property recover the cost with an oath, unless he has eaten from it. This case tests whether using one dinar of her principal counts as eating.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Ruled on the husband's claim and changed his ruling when the Sages objected.

terms.meaning: A place the translation describes as a remote location in Babylonia.
The produce is what property yields, which a husband may enjoy; the principal is the property itself, which stays the wife's.
A sworn statement before the court, used to support a claim when there is no other proof.

11.note: A woman brought two maidservants with her into her marriage. Her husband married a second wife and gave one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came before Rava and cried out, but Rava took no notice of her. Those who saw it thought Rava held that whatever a husband does with his wife's property stands. The Gemara says that is not so: his reason was that the maidservant was still serving the household.
11.why: The Gemara asks whether a husband may sell the produce of his wife's land, and two opposite reports of Rava's view are given. Rav Pappa says the permissive report was only inferred from this case, which the Gemara then reads another way.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who ignored the first wife's protest.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Explains that the permissive report of Rava's view was inferred from this case.

people.name: Yehuda Mar bar Mareimar
people.about: Reported in Rava's name that what a husband does with the produce takes effect.

terms.meaning: The Sages' reason for giving a husband the produce of his wife's property: it is meant to benefit their household.

12.note: Relatives of Rabbi Yoḥanan seized a cow belonging to orphans in an alley, as the translation explains, because the orphans' father had owed them money. They came before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who told them they had seized it rightly. Then they came before Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who told them to go and give it back. They went back to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said: What can I do? One who is my equal disagrees with me.
12.why: The Gemara is weighing why Reish Lakish would reverse judges who ruled like Rabbi Tarfon against Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Yoḥanan would not. Here the two Sages rule opposite ways on just such a seizure.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Approved his relatives' seizure, then deferred to his colleague.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: Also called Reish Lakish; ordered the cow returned to the orphans.

terms.meaning: Here, the heirs of a man who has died, from whose inheritance his creditors try to collect.

13.note: Members of the prince's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans in an alley. Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa were sitting as judges, with Rabbi Abba beside them, and Rabbi Abbahu told the seizers they had taken her rightly. Rabbi Abba objected: because they are of the prince's house, will you flatter them? Judges once ruled like Rabbi Tarfon in such a case, and Reish Lakish reversed their decision. The text does not say how the case ended.
13.why: It is one of a series of cases about seizing orphans' property for their father's debt. Rabbi Abba treats Reish Lakish's reversal, just told, as binding against the ruling that favored the seizers.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of the judges; he upheld the seizure.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi
people.about: Sat as a judge in the case.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: Sat as a judge in the case.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sat with the judges and accused them of flattering the powerful.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Cited for having reversed a ruling that followed Rabbi Tarfon.

terms.meaning: The household of the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, as the translation puts it.
Here, the heirs of a man who died owing money.

14.note: Yeimar bar Ḥashu was owed money by a man who died leaving a boat, and he sent his agent to seize it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him that, by Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule, one who seizes for a creditor at the expense of others acquires nothing. Then they seized the boat themselves: Rav Pappa rowed it and Rav Huna pulled it by a rope, and each said he had acquired all of it. Rav Pineḥas bar Ami objected that seizing counts only for goods lying in the public domain; they said they took it from the river's current. They came before Rava, who called them white geese who strip people of their cloaks, and cited Rav Naḥman: a seizure counts only if made while the debtor was alive.
14.why: The Gemara is gathering cases about creditors who seize a dead debtor's property. This one adds the rule against an agent seizing at others' expense, and ends with Rava's ruling that seizing after the debtor's death acquires nothing.

people.name: Yeimar bar Ḥashu
people.about: A creditor who sent his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Told the agent his seizure was void, then seized the boat himself.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Seized the boat together with Rav Pappa, each claiming all of it.

people.name: Rav Pineḥas bar Ami
people.about: Questioned whether their seizure was valid.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rebuked both Sages and ruled their seizure void.

terms.meaning: Space belonging to no one, such as a street or a river's current. Rav and Shmuel say seizing goods acquires them only if they lie there.
Rava's insult; the translation explains it refers to their white beards.

15.note: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu owed money to people in Bei Ḥozai and sent it with Ḥama son of Rabba bar Abbahu. Ḥama paid them and asked for the loan document back. They said the money had paid other debts, not the one in the document. The case came before Rabbi Abbahu, who asked Ḥama whether he had witnesses that he had paid. He had none. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since they could have said they were never paid at all, they are believed when they say the money went to other debts.
15.why: The Gemara has been collecting cases on debts and claims in court. Right after this one it asks whether the agent, who handed over the money without getting the document back, must repay the man who sent him.

people.name: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Owed money and sent an agent to repay it.

people.name: Ḥama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
people.about: The agent who paid the debt without getting the document.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Judged the case; Avimi's father.

terms.meaning: A rule of evidence: a person is believed in a claim because he could have made a stronger one and did not.
A place in Babylonia.

16.note: A woman was required to take an oath in Rava's court. Rav Ḥisda's daughter, Rava's wife, told him she knew the woman was suspected of swearing falsely, so Rava turned the oath over to the other side. Another time, Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana were sitting before Rava when a document was brought, and Rav Pappa said he knew the debt in it had been paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew; no one did, and Rava said that even with the Master's word, one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked: should Rav Pappa not count at least as much as Rav Ḥisda's daughter? Rava answered: I am certain about her; I am not certain about the Master.
16.why: The surrounding cases concern oaths and debt documents in court. Right after, Rav Pappa takes from Rava's answer that a judge's personal certainty about someone has legal weight, and the Gemara limits it: it may weaken a document, not tear it up.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A judge who relied on his wife's word but not on Rav Pappa's.

people.name: The daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who warned him the woman could not be trusted to swear.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Said he knew a debt document had already been paid.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Asked why Rav Pappa was trusted less than Rav Ḥisda's daughter.

terms.meaning: Instead of the defendant swearing she owes nothing, the other party swears that she does and collects.
Jewish law normally requires two witnesses to establish a fact in court.

17.note: A relative of Rav Naḥman sold the rights to her marriage contract for a sum of money. She was later divorced and died, and the buyers came to claim its value from her daughter. Rav Naḥman said: is there no one to advise her to forgive her mother's marriage contract to her father, and then inherit the money from him? The daughter heard, went and forgave it. Afterward Rav Naḥman said: We have made ourselves like advisers to the litigants. The Gemara explains that at first he held one must not turn away from one's own flesh, and in the end held that an important person is different.
17.why: The Gemara has just cited Shmuel: one who sells a debt document can still forgive the debt, and so can his heir. Rav Naḥman's advice uses exactly that rule to defeat the buyers.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A judge who gave advice to a relative's daughter and then regretted it.

terms.meaning: The document recording what a husband must pay his wife if he divorces her or dies; she could sell her right to collect it.
The translation explains: like lawyers who coach one side rather than independent judges.

18.note: A case arose in which a creditor had sold a debt document and then forgiven the debt. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule, and Rav Ashi made him pay as one who damages a beam meant for carving statues, which the translation explains as the full value of the debt in the document.
18.why: Ameimar has just said that a judge who holds people liable for indirect damage makes such a seller pay the document's full value, while one who does not makes him pay only for the paper. Here Rav Ashi takes the first view.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: Pressed Rav Ashi to give a ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ruled that the full value must be paid.

terms.meaning: Wood meant for carving is worth far more than plain wood; whoever damages it pays its full worth.

19.note: The estate of the house of bar Tzartzur was small at the father's death and later grew in value. The sons of his two wives came before Rav Amram, who told the sons with the larger claim to go and appease the others. They paid no attention. He said: if you do not appease them, I will strike you with a thorn that draws no blood, which the translation explains as excommunication. He sent them to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that just as heirs keep their rights when a large estate shrinks, so they keep them when a small estate grows.
19.why: The mishna lets each wife's sons collect their own mother's marriage contract only if the estate exceeds both contracts by a dinar. The Gemara asks what happens when it fell short at the father's death but later grew, and brings this case as the answer.

people.name: bar Tzartzur
people.about: The man whose estate his sons were dividing.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Urged the sons to settle and threatened them when they refused.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Ruled on the case.

terms.meaning: The sum a husband pledges to his wife; under the mishna's rule her sons could inherit it.
Rav Amram's threat; the translation says it means excommunication.

20.note: A man owed a creditor a thousand dinars. He owned two mansions and sold each for five hundred. The creditor seized one from its buyer and then came to seize the other as well. The buyer took a thousand dinars to him and said: if the house you took is worth a thousand to you, keep it; if not, take the thousand dinars and give up your claim. Rami bar Ḥama thought this was like the mishna's case of orphans who offer to value their father's property a dinar higher. Rava replied: there, the other orphans lose by it; here, does the creditor lose? He lent a thousand and gets a thousand.
20.why: It follows the mishna's rule that orphans cannot raise the value of their father's estate to gain their mother's marriage contract. Rava's answer shows that rule does not stop a buyer's offer that costs the creditor nothing.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Compared the buyer's offer to the mishna's case of the orphans.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rejected the comparison.

terms.meaning: A creditor may take land the debtor sold after the loan, because the debt was secured on the debtor's land.
The core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.
